content: For men aged 18–59 years, clinical evaluation should include a detailed history and assessment of risk factors. In antenatal clinics, this involves a WHO-based history and risk factor evaluation. In well-woman and sexual health clinics, the evaluation includes a WHO-based history, risk factor assessment, and a genital examination. For the detection of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing is recommended. Similarly, Trichomonas vaginalis can also be identified using real-time PCR. Management of Vaginal Discharge in Women Different clinical approaches and flowcharts have been modeled to manage gonorrhea and/or chlamydial infections in women presenting with vaginal discharge. These approaches include: 1. No treatment: No intervention is provided. 2. Treat all: All women are treated empirically for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. 3. Risk-based treatment: Women at high risk, based on a risk assessment, are treated for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. 4. Speculum examination: If signs of cervicitis (e.g., mucopurulent discharge) are observed during a speculum examination, treatment for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is initiated. 5. Speculum examination with microscopy: If the speculum examination is negative, microscopy (Gram stain) is performed. If gram-negative diplococci or >20 pus cells per high-power field are detected, treatment is provided. 6. Point-of-care testing: If the speculum examination is negative, a point-of-care test is performed. If the test is positive, treatment for N. gonorrhoeae and/or C. trachomatis is initiated. 7. Microscopy-first approach: Microscopy (Gram stain) is performed first. If positive, treatment for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is provided. 8. Risk assessment and genital examination: If either the risk assessment or genital examination is positive (e.g., presence of vaginal discharge), treatment is initiated. 9. Low-cost point-of-care testing: Women with positive risk assessments or genital examinations undergo low-cost point-of-care testing. If the test is positive, treatment is provided. 10. High-cost point-of-care testing: In high-risk women, high-cost point-of-care testing is performed. If the test is positive, treatment is initiated. Syndromic Management of Lower Abdominal Pain The WHO syndromic management approach for lower abdominal pain aims to identify and treat pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This approach is compared to laboratory-based diagnosis, no treatment, or treating all cases empirically. Population: Women presenting with lower abdominal pain. Purpose: To identify women requiring treatment for STIs related to PID. Linked treatments: Treatment for infections caused by C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, T. vaginalis, and anaerobic infections. Lower abdominal pain is a nonspecific symptom that can indicate acute PID, which requires immediate attention to prevent complications such as chronic pelvic pain, tubal infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. PID is a polymicrobial infection that may result from STIs or vaginal microbiome dysbiosis. Diagnostic Challenges There is no objective test for PID, and symptoms can range from severe to absent. Clinical diagnosis often involves a bimanual examination to detect cervical and uterine tenderness in women with acute lower pelvic pain, fever, and vaginal or cervical discharge. However, this procedure is invasive, uncomfortable, and subjective, leading to potential missed cases and increased risks of ectopic pregnancy and infertility. Laparoscopy is considered the gold standard for diagnosing PID but is impractical as a routine screening tool. Until more accurate diagnostics are available, clinicians are advised to adopt a low threshold for syndromic management in suspected PID cases. Antimicrobial Resistance There is growing concern about antimicrobial resistance in N. gonorrhoeae, with high rates of resistance to penicillin, tetracycline, and quinolones documented globally. Resistance to first-line medications like azithromycin and reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins (a last-line treatment) further complicates management. Cost Considerations The cost of managing PID varies widely. The average cost in the UK is £163 (range: £96–960), while the average lifetime cost in the US is $2400. Molecular STI testing is more expensive, highlighting the need for affordable, near-patient diagnostic platforms. Evidence and Recommendations The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of syndromic management for symptomatic STIs, particularly in resource-limited settings where laboratory diagnostics may not be accessible. While the syndromic approach may lead to overtreatment, the benefits of timely treatment for true cases of PID outweigh the risks of unnecessary treatment, which generally has minimal side effects.
